name: Tcl
title: Tcl (9.0)

type.text: **No static type checking**: A variable holds any value and a command converts its arguments when it runs, so a type error appears at the point of use rather than at compile time

**No sum types and no generics**: A choice between alternatives is a string, a list, or a `dict` with a discriminating key, and a `proc` declares no type parameter, so neither the alternative read nor the types a body expects are checked (T4, T5)
**No null-safety**: There is no null type; an empty string, an empty list, and an unset variable are distinct states, and `$x` on an unset variable aborts the script

**One global namespace and no module boundary**: A `proc` declared at the top level is a global command, `namespace eval` is opt-in, and `source` evaluates a file into the current interpreter without restricting what that file makes visible (T6, T11)

**A protocol is not a declared type**: TclOO, in the core since 8.6, provides classes, mixins, and multiple inheritance, so a shared protocol is captured by a class hierarchy or a mixin rather than by an interface the interpreter checks
**A value's subtype is inspectable**: `string is` and the `expr` conversions such as `int()`, `double()`, and `boolean()` let a script test a value before it is used

construction.text: **Global state appears at the first assignment**: At the top level a name becomes a global variable when it is assigned, so two scripts in one interpreter share those variables
**Nothing is immutable**: `set` is the only declaration a variable receives, and it can reassign or `unset` the value at any time
**No constructor or validation hook**: A value is whatever a command stored, and a `proc` cannot reject a malformed argument unless it checks by hand

**`proc` gives a body its own local scope**: A procedure is a named command with a parameter list, and its parameters and locals do not touch a caller's variables unless `global`, `variable`, or `upvar` says so
**`namespace eval` gives a scope of its own**: A namespace holds its own variables and commands, so a package need not write into the global scope

**`upvar` and `uplevel` reach into the caller's frame**: A procedure that binds a caller's variable, or evaluates in the caller's scope, depends on where it was called from, and `global` and `variable` make a shared variable explicit but still shared

memory.text: **The interpreter owns the heap**: There is no allocate or free command, and a script never names an address
**A value is reclaimed when its last reference goes away**: Reference counting releases a `Tcl_Obj` without a lifetime written in the script
**The dual representation keeps a compiled form beside the string**: A `Tcl_Obj` holds its string and, once used as a list or an integer, an internal representation that is reused
**A C extension allocates through the interpreter**: An extension uses `Tcl_Alloc` and `Tcl_Free`, so the interpreter's accounting still applies

**A reference cycle is not reclaimed by counting alone**: Two objects that reference each other are released only by the interpreter's cycle collection, and a cycle held by an extension is not collected at all
**Taking the string form discards the internal representation**: An operation that needs the string regenerates it, so a hot loop can pay the same conversion more than once

error.text: **A failure can be ignored by design**: `catch` returns a status and nothing requires the caller to test it, so an unchecked return value discards the failure
**Every failure is a value**: `catch` returns a status such as `ok`, `error`, `return`, `break`, or `continue`, together with the result and the error options
**`errorInfo` and `errorCode` carry the detail**: After an error the interpreter records the stack trace and a machine-readable code such as `POSIX ENOENT`
**`error` raises and `return -code` states a status**: A command states the status it wants to propagate to its caller
**A handler that matches the message text is bound to the wording**: The message is a string, and `errorCode` is the documented field to test instead
**`catch` also catches `return` and `break`**: A nested return arrives as a status, so it must be passed on deliberately rather than by accident

concurrency.text: **I/O is a channel**: `chan` reads and writes a stream, so a program composes I/O without naming a file descriptor
**`after` and `vwait` give an event loop**: A callback runs on the interpreter's event loop, and the script does not block the process while it waits
**Coroutines are in the core since Tcl 8.6**: `coroutine`, `yield`, and `tailcall` express a suspendable computation as an ordinary command
**Threads are available when the core is built with them**: Each thread runs its own interpreter and threads exchange values through a thread-safe channel queue rather than shared variables
**A script runs on the thread that calls it**: One `Tcl_Interp` is not usable from two threads at once, so state is partitioned per thread
**A callback can outlive its intended state**: An `after` script or a channel handler holds the interpreter's state, so a cancelled operation must be cancelled explicitly

platform.text: **One implementation is portable across platforms**: The core builds and runs on Windows, macOS, and Unix-like systems from one source base
**Embedding is a first-class use**: The C API (`Tcl_CreateInterp`, `Tcl_Eval`, `Tcl_CreateObjCommand`) lets a host application embed an interpreter and expose its own commands
**A script needs no build step**: A `.tcl` file runs as written through `tclsh`
**The implementation is one project**: Tcl and Tk are maintained by a single core team that sets the language direction, so the platform has one centre
**Tk and every extension are separate packages**: GUI work requires Tk beside the core, and a package must be found on `auto_path` or `TCLLIBPATH`
**A native extension is built per platform**: A package that wraps a C library ships a compiled binary for each target, and the binary must match the interpreter version

performance.text: **The core compiles a script to bytecode**: The bytecode compiler added in the 8.x series means a loop body is not re-parsed at each iteration
**`expr` compiles arithmetic**: An expression is compiled to instructions rather than dispatched as a sequence of commands
**A C extension removes the interpreter from the hot path**: A command implemented in C runs compiled code, which is how performance-critical work is normally done
**Each command still costs a dispatch**: A loop written in Tcl pays parse and dispatch overhead per iteration, so the speed comes from moving the loop into C or into `expr` and `string` operations
**A re-generated string form costs again**: An operation that needs the string representation discards the internal one, so a hot loop can convert repeatedly
**Tk redraw bounds GUI throughput**: A large widget tree redraws at the rate the toolkit can service it

ecosystem.text: **The ecosystem is small and largely legacy**: The active package field is far smaller than that of a mainstream language, and much Tcl code still in use was written decades ago
**Tcllib and Tklib are maintained standard libraries**: Pure-Tcl packages for containers, lists, and protocols, distributed separately from the core
**The distribution is a complete tool**: `tclsh` and `wish` need nothing else installed to run a script
**A package system names and resolves packages**: `package provide`, `package require`, and the `teacup` distribution machinery locate and version a package
**A binary package is distributed per platform**: A compiled extension must match the platform and the interpreter version, so a pure-Tcl package travels more easily
**The documentation corpus is stable but old**: The manual pages are complete, and most tutorials and examples date from the 1990s and 2000s

**A compiled extension binds to a release line**: Tcl states that extensions built against 8.6 and before will not work with 9.0, and ABI compatibility was a non-goal for 9.0 [@tclTk90; @tclStubLayer]

evolution.text: **Tcl 9.0 is an actively released line**: Tcl/Tk 9.0 appeared in September 2024 after the long 8.x series, and 9.0.x maintenance releases continue
**Scripts are largely backward compatible**: The migration notes list a small set of removed pre-8.0 legacies such as the old `case`, `puts`, and `read` forms
**Tcl 9.0 broke the C extension interface**: `Tcl_Size` replaced `int` for lengths and indices and `Tcl_UniChar` became 32-bit, so an extension built for 8.6 must be rebuilt
**A major release arrives rarely**: 9.0 came 27 years after 8.0, so a core change can wait a long time
**The project publishes a migration guide for scripts and for extensions**: "Migrating scripts to Tcl 9" and "Migrating C extensions to Tcl 9" state each required change

domain.text: **Embedded scripting is the native domain**: A C or C++ host embeds an interpreter and exposes its own commands, which is how Tcl is most often used
**Tk is a mature cross-platform GUI toolkit**: Tcl/Tk remains a workable choice for a simple desktop GUI
**Expect automates an interactive program**: The Expect extension drives a terminal program through its prompts and is the standard tool for that job
**Tcl is used as a test and build harness**: The core's own test suite and many command-line tools use a Tcl driver
**General application work is rare**: Outside embedded scripting, GUI, and automation a new project rarely chooses Tcl
**The heavy computation is normally in C**: A Tcl program is usually a thin layer over an extension that does the work

learning.text: **The syntax is tiny**: A script is a sequence of commands, and `set`, `proc`, `if`, and `foreach` cover most of the surface
**The manual is uniform**: Every command has a manual page with the same sections, so the reference is easy to navigate
**An interactive shell is part of the tool**: `tclsh` evaluates a line as it is typed, so an experiment is immediate
**Substitution and quoting need care**: `$var`, `[command]`, braces, and backslash interact, so a command that builds another command is a skill of its own
**The single-value model surprises a newcomer**: A list, a number, and a script are values of one kind, and the difference appears only when a command interprets the value
**The object systems are additional**: TclOO is built in and [incr Tcl] is an extension, so object-oriented Tcl is a layer above the command core

syntax.text: **A command is words separated by whitespace**: `puts hello` is a command with one argument, and the language uses almost no operator punctuation
**Braces group a block without substitution**: `{ ... }` passes the enclosed text unevaluated, which is how `if`, `proc`, and `foreach` receive a body
**A script is data**: Because a script is a list of words, a command can build and evaluate one
**`expr` has its own grammar**: An expression uses operators and functions rather than command words, so the syntax changes inside its braces
**Substitution is dense**: `$`, `[`, and `\` each start a substitution, and a missing escape changes the meaning of a line
**An unbalanced brace or bracket changes the parse**: A newline ends a command, so an unclosed group swallows the following lines

testing.text: **`tcltest` is part of the core**: The standard test package supplies `test`, `testConstraint`, and a summary, so a suite needs no external framework
**A test is a script the same interpreter runs**: The check and the code under test share one language
**`catch` makes a failure assertable**: A test states the expected status and message, and the return value of `catch` is the assertion
**`trace` observes a variable or a command**: A test can watch a variable write or a command call without changing the code
**`tclsh` is the debugger**: An interactive shell with `info` and `trace` exposes the state without a separate tool
**Nothing checks a command before it runs**: A misspelled command name or a wrong argument count appears only when that line executes

security.text: **Untrusted input can become code**: `eval`, `subst`, `uplevel`, and `expr` evaluate text, so a value built from input can be executed as a command

**The single-value model cannot reject a malformed input at the boundary**: Because every value is a string, an injection that forms a valid command is not distinguishable from a legitimate one by the type system
**A safe interpreter removes the dangerous commands**: `interp create -safe` makes an interpreter without `exec`, `open`, `source`, and `load`
**A host can define the whole command surface**: An embedded interpreter exposes only the commands the host creates, which is the usual Tcl sandbox
**`catch` and `error` bound a failure**: A failing command can be reported instead of ending the interpreter
**Correct quoting is the mitigation and it must be uniform**: `list` and `lindex` build a command safely, but only at every site where input becomes code

tradeoffs: **Everything is a string is a design choice**: One representation for scripts, lists, and data buys uniform introspection at a conversion cost
**A command is the only abstraction**: The language has no operator table and no macro layer, so a domain language is built by writing commands
**A small core plus packages is a scope decision**: Tcllib, Tk, and Expect are separate distributions, and a program chooses which to depend on
**There is no compile step by design**: A syntax error appears when the script reaches the command
**Tcl 9.0 treats compatibility with 8.6 extensions as a non-goal**: The project states that ABI compatibility was not an aim, so the rebuild cost is a stated trade rather than an accident
**A Tcl program is meant to be a layer over a host**: The design point is a C or C++ program with a Tcl configuration and control layer
verdict: Tcl's design yields a moderate core score, and its losses cluster where declaration is absent: the type is dynamic, a variable defaults to the global scope, and nothing is immutable or validated. What the language does provide is a small, uniform command core that separates a procedure from its call sites, a real namespace construct with `namespace eval`, and an interpreter that manages memory for the script. Main strengths: embedding through the C API, the mature Tk toolkit, the built-in `tcltest` package, and a bytecode compiler that keeps the loop cost off the parser. Main weaknesses: everything is a string, so injection is an inherent risk and no type error is caught before run time; the implementation is a single project; the ecosystem is small and largely legacy; and the upgrade to Tcl 9.0 obliges every compiled extension to be rebuilt.

energy.text: Interpreted by default: the slowest class in the energy and time benchmarks [@pereira2017energy]; a causal re-analysis attributes most of the gap to execution time [@vankempen2025green].

ai-readiness.text: Sparse training data: models write it unreliably [@joel2025lowresource].

safety.text: No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

delivery.note: A Tcl package ships source the interpreter parses
